implementation_notes: Python has no compile-time copy semantics to delete: `copy.copy` duplicates almost anything, `copy.deepcopy` follows the same hooks, and the pickling protocol offers a third duplication path - so the mixin becomes hand-written runtime guards on every entry point. Define `__copy__` and `__deepcopy__` to raise `TypeError`, block the pickling route (`__reduce_ex__`/`__getstate__`, or a `copyreg` registration), keep identity equality (do not define `__eq__`), close the attribute set with `__slots__`, and construct only through a module-level factory while the class itself stays private by convention. The classic base-class form has no Python equivalent; what remains is a documented convention - a subclass or `object.__new__` can still produce a second instance, so the guard stops accidental duplication, not a determined caller.
pitfalls: Guarding only `__copy__` leaves `copy.deepcopy`, `pickle` and `__reduce_ex__` as copy paths; block the pickling protocol too or state that the guarantee is shallow-only.

`__slots__` closes `__dict__` for this class, but a subclass can re-open it and can also override `__copy__` back to a working implementation, so pair the guard with a factory and a documented 'do not subclass' contract.
Raising from `__deepcopy__` breaks any `copy.deepcopy` of a structure that contains the object (caches, deep-copied configuration), so the failure surfaces far from the copy site.
Private-by-convention attributes are not enforcement: `object.__new__` plus attribute assignment still builds a second instance, so treat the guard as an accident barrier, not a security boundary.
